item.title: 2027 Cybersecurity Excellence Awards Launch With Six New AI Security Categories
item.description:
San Francisco, USA, November 17th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Global awards program invites nominations across more than 100 cybersecurity categories, with early-bird pricing through Cyber Monday.

The Cybersecurity Excellence Awards, presented by Cybersecurity Insiders, announced the official launch of its 2027 awards season, inviting cybersecurity companies, innovators, professionals, and teams worldwide to submit their achievements for independent recognition. Submit a nomination: https://cybersecurity-excellence-awards.com/

The 2027 season introduces six new AI security categories: AI Security Posture Management (AI-SPM), AI Red Teaming, MCP Security, Guardian Agents, AI Usage Control, and AI Supply Chain Security.

“In 2024, AI security was one award category. For 2027, we have 18 dedicated categories, because securing AI agents with access to business systems is a different challenge from stopping AI-enabled attacks,” said Holger Schulze, founder and CEO of Cybersecurity Insiders. “We want to recognize excellence in each, rather than treating AI security as one market.”

Recognition Across the Cybersecurity Industry

The awards cover cybersecurity products and services, companies, industry solutions, and professionals and teams. Categories span emerging fields such as post-quantum cryptography (PQC) alongside established disciplines including network security, Zero Trust, identity, data security, endpoint protection, and cyber resilience.

Independent cybersecurity judges evaluate nominations based on leadership, innovation, and impact, comparing achievements against relevant peers.

Every approved nomination also enters Community Choice, a separate public vote that does not influence jury results. Outstanding Gold winners may be considered for Best in Class distinctions throughout the year, without requiring another nomination.

Nominations and Key Dates

The 2027 Nomination Guide explains award categories, judging criteria, entry requirements, and pricing. Nominees can save their work and complete submissions later.

Early-bird pricing is available through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, for entries paid by the deadline. Nominations close February 27, 2027. Jury award winners will be announced the week of March 22, ahead of the RSAC Conference, with Community Choice winners announced in July, ahead of Black Hat USA.

Submit a nomination: https://cybersecurity-excellence-awards.com/

Read the Nomination Guide: https://cybersecurity-excellence-awards.com/nomination-guide/

About the Cybersecurity Excellence Awards

For more than a decade, the Cybersecurity Excellence Awards have recognized excellence, innovation, and leadership across the cybersecurity industry. The program is presented by Cybersecurity Insiders, a research and media platform backed by a community of more than 600,000 cybersecurity professionals worldwide.

item.title: FBI Says ARTEX AI Tool Helped Hackers Gain Privileged Access in Under 3 Hours
item.description:
The FBI is warning about a new framework, ARTEX, which automates several stages of a cyberattack, from finding targets to stealing data.

In a November 13 Flash Advisory, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said cybercriminals had been using the open-source framework since at least August 2026 to target organizations worldwide. The targeted sectors include financial services, government, technology, defense, healthcare, semiconductor, energy, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal services.

One confirmed incident involved a supply-chain compromise of ConnectWise Cloud Backup that allowed attackers to access more than 2,250 downstream tenants.

Written in Go, ARTEX connects to external large language models (LLMs) like DeepSeek, Claude and GPT. What makes it different is its use of specialized AI agents that work on separate tasks after an operator sets an objective. These agents can identify targets, check systems for weaknesses, exploit them and exfiltrate data, with little human involvement.

The FBI says (PDF) some attacks have moved from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours and that DeepSeek Flash models are particularly popular among attackers because of their relatively low cost and lack of observable safety guardrails for penetration testing.

The problem goes beyond faster attacks

Some ARTEX-assisted intrusions have reached privileged access in less than three hours. That leaves security teams little time to investigate an intrusion before attackers move further into a network. The ConnectWise incident shows how this can affect other organizations.

Microsoft’s investigation into Artex linked the activity to Storm-0940, a China-aligned threat group. After compromising ConnectWise applications, the attackers used the access to target customer environments. Microsoft also recorded more than 151,000 failed sign-in attempts during a related campaign, with activity reaching 2,900 attempts per minute.

The FBI also highlighted attacks against South Korean financial institutions in which personal information of around 67,000 people was stolen. Impacted banks included Shinhan, KB Kookmin, Hana, BNK Busan Banks, Hyundai Capital, Yegaram Savings Bank, and Welcome Savings Bank among others.

These findings highlight the gradual change in the way attackers are using AI. Hackread.com previously reported on a PaperCut campaign in which hundreds of AI agents helped attackers develop, troubleshoot and scale the exploitation of two zero-day vulnerabilities. ARTEX brings several attack stages together in a single framework. This further reduces the work needed to move between them.

Google’s threat intelligence team has also reported malicious use of other agentic frameworks, including CAIRN and PentAGI. Its findings suggest that these operations can be noisy and relatively unsophisticated but still successful because of their speed and scale.

Taking down the original tool did not end its use

ARTEX’s developer, Autumn-27, removed the original GitHub repository on October 8, 2026, following reports of abuse. But copies, community forks and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO remain available with more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles identified by early November.

The FBI is seeking authentication records, API activity, cloud logs and other evidence of ARTEX-related attacks.

The FBI’s findings have also raised concerns about how organizations manage exposed systems, credentials and access between suppliers. Morey J. Haber, Chief Security Advisor at BeyondTrust, shared with Hackread.com that ARTEX changes the time and expertise needed to turn discovered weaknesses into working attacks.

“The truth, however, is not about a new exploit or zero-day vulnerability developed by AI. It is the collapse of the time and the expertise barrier between what is discovered and when it is weaponized. Threat actors have long known that the weakest link is not always on a flagship application. A successful breach can occur in a partner portal, a legacy service, a backend mobile application, or a forgotten third-party integration. Until now, finding and chaining those dependencies took effort, talent, and time. ARTEX industrializes these concepts.”

Haber also warned that organizations should pay closer attention to identities and credentials used by applications and automated services, not just employee accounts.

“ARTEX is not breaking in so much as logging in with keys it finds lying around, including machine identities and service accounts that nobody is monitoring or that have been forgotten about. And since it maps trust between organizations, your risk is only as strong as your weakest supplier. Put simply, the blast radius extends well beyond your own perimeter.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: After Black October, OffSec Turns PHPH2Shell and Other New Vulnerabilities Into Hands-On Labs
item.description:
New York City, United States, November 18th, 2026, CyberNewswire

OffSec built 14 labs on real CVEs in two weeks. Its Level 20 offer takes $550 off Learn One for learners ready to train against threats like these.

OffSec, the world’s leading provider of hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications, released more than 80 hands-on labs in the last two weeks of October as Black October crippled government and university websites across Europe. The labs give security teams a safe place to attack and defend the same kinds of flaws making headlines. Fourteen are built on real CVEs disclosed this year. They include a free lab on PHP2Shell, the PHP flaw at the center of the month’s disclosure wave.

Black October is the name the security community gave to a cluster of critical disclosures in late October. At its center was PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The flaws let attackers run code on web servers without logging in. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws with help from AI models. Amazon spotted an exploitation attempt on Oct. 17, four days before public disclosure. CERT-EU told organizations that could not patch right away to isolate internet-facing apps from public networks. CISA urged immediate patching. The same day GitLab patched a maximum-severity flaw that let unauthenticated users run code on its servers. CrowdStrike reported four threat actors running campaigns in which AI agents make decisions and execute commands.

The pace reflects a larger shift. AI now helps find flaws and turn them into working exploits. An AI agent can compare a vulnerable release against its patched version and see exactly what changed. That shrinks the window defenders have to understand a flaw and act on it.

“AI has lowered the skill ceiling for attackers,” said Alex “Sickness” Uifalvi, Security Researcher and architect at OffSec. “Going from a patch to a working exploit used to take a skilled team up to a week. An agent can cut that by a big chunk. Defenders need to get their hands on these flaws while they are still in the news. That is why our team builds labs on real CVEs as fast as we can. You learn what an attack looks like by running it and stopping it yourself.”

OffSec’s new labs, listed in its Oct. 19–25 and Oct. 26–Nov. 2 weekly updates, cover both sides of an incident, and include:

  • Offensive Labs built on recent CVEs in Kestra, Hermes WebUI, WordPress 7.0.2, the Algernon web server and a chained Vite and Uptime Kuma exposure.
  • Defensive Labs where learners secure vulnerable versions of Spring, Kestra and Next.js.
  • Incident Investigations modeled on real attack types. These include ransomware that began with a help desk call, an email compromise that rerouted a client payment, a breached SSL VPN appliance and an intrusion at a hydroelectric plant.
  • AI Targets such as an AI-driven tool marketplace with an automated reviewer and agent.

OffSec CEO Ning Wang said fast-moving flaws like PHP2Shell are now the norm.

“These vulnerabilities are being found by AI agents and that will happen more and more,” said CEO Wang. “You need to very quickly understand how a flaw works and how to defend against it. When PHP2Shell hit, we acted instantly to develop a new lab and a blog to begin teaching people how the attack works and how to stop it. Every organization that cares about its business risk needs to be on top of these things. Your red team and your blue team both need to know how to use AI to do their jobs. It’s no longer a nice-to-do. It’s a must-do.”

Level 20: Same Game, New Level

OffSec is marking 20 years of hands-on training with Level 20, a year-end offer for individual learners. Learn One is $550 off through Jan. 4, 2027. Security professionals who want to learn AI red teaming can now train for OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer) through Learn One. This is the first time OSAI is part of a Learn One offer. Its AI-300 course covers attacks on AI models, large language models and autonomous agents.

A Learn One Subscription Includes:

  • One 200- or 300-level OffSec course such as PEN-200 for the OSCP penetration testing certification or AI-300 for OSAI
  • 365 days of course and lab access
  • Two attempts at the certification exam
  • More than 200 Proving Grounds Practice labs
  • Bonus KLCP and OSWP courses and exams

The PHP2Shell lab is free to use on Proving Grounds Play. Claim the Level 20 offer at learn.offsec.com/level-20-promo.

About OffSec

OffSec (formerly Offensive Security) is the world’s leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications. Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

From its beginnings to today, OffSec has set the elite standard for cybersecurity proficiency, earning global recognition and the implicit trust of the world’s most elite security teams. With a comprehensive ecosystem ranging from the industry-defining OSCP to the cutting-edge OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer), OffSec is the definitive benchmark for validating real-world technical skills in an increasingly automated world.

item.title: Fast People Search Removal (2026): How to Opt Out & Remove Yourself
item.description:
Anyone can type your name into FastPeopleSearch and see your age, your current address, your phone numbers, and who your relatives are. No account, no fee. Have you checked what it says about you?

The opt-out steps come first, since that’s why you’re here. After that, we’ll look at why the listing is a security risk and how to stop it from creeping back. The steps match the site’s current opt-out form, so you can get your listing taken down today.

How to remove yourself from FastPeopleSearch

Good news first: it’s free, and you don’t need to dig up your own listing beforehand, because FastPeopleSearch finds it from the details you give it.

  1. Go straight to fastpeoplesearch.com/optout. Searching for yourself on the homepage only brings up listings, which won’t get you to the form.
  2. Fill in the first form. Type your first and last name and an email address you can open right away, then tick the consent box and solve the captcha before you hit submit.
  3. Open the email link. FastPeopleSearch then emails you a link to a second form. The link stops working after 24 hours, so it’s easiest to do both forms in one go.
  4. Complete the second form. Add either your date of birth or your street address (you only need one), plus your city, state, and ZIP code, then submit. The form may also ask for a phone number. A confirmation shows up on screen, and another lands in your inbox.

Not sure you’re on the right screen? This fast people search removal walkthrough has screenshots for every step. Two more things make this go smoother:

  • Use a personal email address. Work inboxes often sit behind spam filters that can quietly swallow verification emails.
  • Double-check the second form before you submit it, because there’s no way to edit it afterward. It’s also worth screenshotting the confirmation page.

Why a free people-search listing is a security risk

People usually talk about these sites as a privacy issue. For scammers, though, a listing like this is a cheat sheet. Think about what a fake “bank” caller or a phishing email needs to sound believable: your name, where you live, maybe a relative or two. FastPeopleSearch hands over all of that. Your address and phone number also help someone pose as you when they call customer support about your accounts.

People reported losing $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025, according to the FTC, and fake bank alerts were behind some of the most expensive ones. The agency’s guide to family emergency scams also warns that the caller may already know your name and where you live. Would you hang up on a caller who already knew your address and your mother’s name?

When it doesn’t work

If something goes wrong, it’s usually one of these:

  • The email never shows up. Check spam and promotions. Still nothing after half an hour? Start over, since the link may have expired.
  • You’re still listed after 3 days. Search again in a private window, in case your browser is showing an old copy. Then check FastPeopleSearch’s email to see whether the removal worked, and if it didn’t, resend the request carefully. Typos are the usual problem.
  • You have more than one listing. Old addresses or a maiden name can each create a separate profile, and each needs its own request.
  • You still appear on a relative’s profile. Removing your own listing doesn’t take your name off reports about your relatives or neighbors, so check those too.
  • It’s gone from FastPeopleSearch but still on Google. That’s an old copy Google hasn’t updated yet. You can ask Google to refresh outdated content by pasting in the old listing’s link.

Why your listing comes back

Here’s the annoying part. FastPeopleSearch doesn’t stop collecting after you opt out. It keeps pulling in public records and commercial data, so a move, a new phone number, a home purchase, or even an updated voter registration can put a fresh profile back online, sometimes months later.

Is any of this legal? In the US, mostly yes, although some state privacy laws give residents more say, such as the right to stop a company from selling their data. So don’t think of removal as a one-off. Search your name every few months and repeat the opt-out if you pop up again.

It’s not the only site with your data

Opting out of FastPeopleSearch only covers FastPeopleSearch. Lots of similar sites use the same kinds of records, and each has its own opt-out form. Search your name on two or three big ones, like TruePeopleSearch, Spokeo, or Whitepages, and opt out wherever you show up. It’s tedious, but every removal means one less copy that can leak.

Leaks do happen. In 2024, 2.9 billion records from background-check firm National Public Data ended up on a hacking forum. It was one of the biggest leaks in recent years, but far from the only one.

Conclusion

That’s really all there is to it. You know how to get your FastPeopleSearch listing removed and how to spot it when it comes back. Leave it up, and a scammer gets your address, phone number, and family names for free.

So do the opt-out today, and set a reminder to check again in three months. It’s ten minutes well spent.

  • It’s gone from FastPeopleSearch but still on Google. That’s an old copy Google hasn’t updated yet. You can ask Google to refresh outdated content by pasting in the old listing’s link.

Why your listing comes back

Here’s the annoying part. FastPeopleSearch doesn’t stop collecting after you opt out. It keeps pulling in public records and commercial data, so a move, a new phone number, a home purchase, or even an updated voter registration can put a fresh profile back online, sometimes months later.

Is any of this legal? In the US, mostly yes, although some state privacy laws give residents more say, such as the right to stop a company from selling their data. So don’t think of removal as a one-off. Search your name every few months and repeat the opt-out if you pop up again.

It’s not the only site with your data

Opting out of FastPeopleSearch only covers FastPeopleSearch. Lots of similar sites use the same kinds of records, and each has its own opt-out form. Search your name on two or three big ones, like TruePeopleSearch, Spokeo, or Whitepages, and opt out wherever you show up. It’s tedious, but every removal means one less copy that can leak.

Leaks do happen. In 2024, 2.9 billion records from background-check firm National Public Data ended up on a hacking forum. It was one of the biggest leaks in recent years, but far from the only one.

Conclusion

That’s really all there is to it. You know how to get your FastPeopleSearch listing removed and how to spot it when it comes back. Leave it up, and a scammer gets your address, phone number, and family names for free.

So do the opt-out today, and set a reminder to check again in three months. It’s ten minutes well spent.

item.title: Java4Shell Flaw Lets Attackers Target Java Servers Without Logging In
item.description:
Oracle has released fixes for Java4Shell, a memory-corruption vulnerability that researchers say they used to execute code on several enterprise applications without logging in.

Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the flaw affects hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding in certain Java runtimes. Exposure depends on the Java build, processor and application, so running Java does not automatically make a server vulnerable.

Researchers at Calif assigned it a critical CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. Oracle’s November security advisory separately rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1, with high attack complexity and no authentication or user interaction required. The scores use different versions of the assessment system.

A decoder error inside the Java runtime

Applications use Base64 to represent binary information as text, including in authentication messages and file transfers. On supported processors, OpenJDK speeds up decoding with specialised machine instructions.

According to Calif’s technical report, malformed input can cause that accelerated routine to write outside its allocated memory. Java subsequently rejects the input, but neighbouring memory may already have been corrupted.

Calif says it developed ways to turn the corruption into memory disclosure and remote code execution. Its comparison with Heartbleed concerns the ability to read sensitive memory, not an identical underlying bug.

During its testing, Calif reports achieving pre-authentication code execution against Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It also reports post-authentication exploitation of Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Those are the researchers’ findings, not evidence that every installation of those products is exploitable. Calif says each application needs a tailored exploit and is withholding the product-specific chains while organisations update.

Check the processor as well as the Java version

Two servers running the same Java build can have different exposure because of their processors. Calif says the vulnerable decoder uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions on compatible x86-64 chips. ARM64 processors are unaffected.

Companies also need to check Java runtimes supplied inside applications and container images. Updating a separately installed system JDK does not establish that those bundled copies have changed.

The table below lists the Java versions affected by Java4Shell:

Standard Java 8, Java 11 and Java 17.0.0 through 17.0.5 do not contain the vulnerable decoder described in the research. These exclusions concern Java4Shell specifically and do not mean older releases are safe from other vulnerabilities.

Oracle also lists affected GraalVM products in its advisory. Organisations using another OpenJDK distribution should obtain the corresponding fix from that supplier, since package names and release identifiers differ.

Researchers report code execution, with limits

Dom Glavach, chief information security officer at application security company Black Duck, said companies should act on the available fixes while keeping the reported exploit results in context.

“Oracle has confirmed the flaw and shipped fixes. The discoverers report they turned it into code execution against well-known enterprise products without logging in,” Glavach told Hackread.com.

He noted that the researchers are withholding those chains and that he said he had not seen independent confirmation of the product-specific exploits. Glavach also advised companies to prioritise internet-facing identity and build systems and avoid unverified fixes or purported exploits circulating online.

Apply the runtime update, then restart the application

Companies should obtain a patched Java runtime from their supplier, check which runtime each application actually launches and restart affected services after replacement. Applications with vendor-managed Java installations may require an application update or specific vendor instructions.

Where an update cannot be installed immediately, Calif recommends starting the runtime with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the accelerated Base64 routines. It also lists -XX:UseAVX=2 as an alternative on x86-64 systems, while warning that this second option prevents OpenJDK from starting on ARM.

Administrators should test any temporary startup change with the application vendor. Disabling the vulnerable optimisation can reduce exposure while a patch is arranged, but companies still need to replace affected runtimes, including copies packaged inside applications and containers.

item.title: OX Security Launches OX Radar and Response Center to Show Companies Which Cyber Threats Actually Affect Them
item.description:
New York, United States, November 18th, 2026, TechnologyWire

New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation

OX Security, a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation.

OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain.

When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical.

“The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate. Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.”

From Breaking Threats to Customer Action

To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes. The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs.

The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability. It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected.

Through the Response Center, security teams can:

  • Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge.
  • Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence.
  • Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability.
  • Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests.
  • Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity.

﻿

For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required. Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL.

Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research

Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings. Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time.

Availability

OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website.

About OX Security

OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime. Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments.

Head of Communications
Jillian Jones
OX Security

item.title: Armornet Debuts AI Security for the Code and Vendors Companies Trust
item.description:
Grand Rapids, Michigan, November 18th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Startup shows teams the vendors they rely on, keeps a live risk score on each one and secures the software supply chain from end to end

Armornet, an AI cybersecurity company, is accepting teams into the private alpha of its platform, which gives an automatically discovered, continuous view of the vendors a company’s teams relies on.

Procurement and risk review each vendor at signing. First- and third-party engineering teams ship thousands of lines of code a day. As that code changes, so does how teams use each vendor and where that vendor stands on breaches, exploits and patching. The review done at signing captures none of it.

After teams connect their version control, compliance and workspace tools, Armornet lists the vendors and packages they rely on and how they use them. Armornet’s Agent Mesh monitors everything from package installs to the breach notifications, counting each block and response against the vendor’s risk score. 

Open-source malware grew 75% in 2025, according to Sonatype’s 2026 State of the Software Supply Chain report. In May, GitHub said a hacking group took about 3,800 of its internal repositories through a poisoned code-editor extension on an employee’s device.

“A vendor review is a snapshot, but vendor risk changes every day. Breaches, exploits and patches keep coming, and the teams relying on that vendor are typically the last to find out,” said Tony Ramos, founder and CEO of Armornet. “Armornet gives procurement, security and engineering teams one shared, continuously monitored record of each vendor they rely on, so everyone works from the same picture.”

To enhance developer security skillsets, Armornet offers a growing suite of free-to-play, open-source cybersecurity games. Designed for a range of experience levels, the games turn real-world cybersecurity concepts and software supply chain threats into interactive, hands-on challenges. Anyone can play at armornet.io/breach.

Teams can request alpha access at armornet.io/alpha.

About Armornet

Armornet is an AI cybersecurity company focused on securing the software supply chain, bringing visibility and control of the code, tools and third parties that introduce risk into an organization. The Grand Rapids, Michigan-based company was founded in 2026. Learn more at armornet.io.

item.title: What a GitHub Actions Cache Can Expose to Anyone Who Opens a Pull Request
item.description:
The GitHub Actions cache is commonly used as a timesaver in the dev community. It allows developers to shortcut the laborious process of downloading and installing dependencies and having to rebuild outputs, which makes builds faster and cheaper. While this is certainly praiseworthy, it can create a loophole for malicious actors to exploit.

GitHub lets pull request runs restore caches from the base branch, and that includes pull requests opened from forks, by people outside your team. That means that if you’re running a public repository, anyone can create a fork and read whatever has been cached on the main branch. Even with private repositories, anyone with read access can run the same stunt, which could be an enormous number of people if you aren’t careful about rescinding permissions.

This is not just a theoretical danger. The GhostAction campaign showed how attractive CI credentials are. Attackers read projects’ existing workflow files to learn which secrets they used, then committed malicious workflows with those secret names hardcoded to steal them.

To be fair, your GitHub Actions cache is not necessarily a problem unto itself. It’s still a smart way to make dev workflows more efficient. The problem arises when people are careless about what gets stored in cached paths. A pull request with no access to secrets whatsoever can still read them if those credentials are bundled together in a cache.

GitHub won’t pass secrets to untrusted workflows from forks, and the GITHUB_TOKEN there is read-only, so malicious workflows can’t use it to make unauthorized changes. But GitHub is quite clear that anyone with read access to a repository can create a pull request and access the content of a cache. It’s equally open in warning users that forks can create pull requests and access caches on a base branch.

There are safeguards in place. Caches that are created by a pull request can only be restored by reruns of the same request, which protects the main from being poisoned by a maliciously created cache. There’s also no way to edit a cache after it’s been created, so attackers can’t adapt an existing cache and use that to insert malicious content.

Neither safeguard limits reading, though. If secrets have been written into a cached path on main, a fork’s workflow can restore them without ever having access to the secrets themselves.

Credentials That End Up in Cached Paths

Keeping secrets out of GitHub Actions caches is a long-known best practice. GitHub itself warns against storing sensitive data in cached paths because of the risk of access from pull request workflows. The trouble is that secrets can end up in caches unintentionally, especially when dev teams aren’t warned to look out for this security risk.

There are many ways that secrets can lodge in caches. Most often, it’s because cache paths are too broad, like someone cached the entire home directory or the full workspace to raise the cache hit rate.

The docker login command, for example, saves registry credentials to ~/.docker/config.json by default, so later commands can pull and push images without logging in again. Package manager config files may hold authentication tokens to access private packages, and cloud command-line tools store credentials locally too, the AWS CLI in ~/.aws and the Azure CLI in ~/.azure. API keys, passwords, and other environment variable values can be stored in .env files or embedded in build outputs and cached by mistake.

Why a Leaked Cache Entry Stays Dangerous

It’s true that GitHub regularly clears out cache entries. Anything that hasn’t been accessed for seven days gets deleted as a matter of course.

But that is not the same as removing credentials. If a pull request restores a cache, the credentials come along with it and can be copied anywhere you like.

And those credentials are most likely still active and effective. One recent report found that 64% of valid secrets from 2022 were still not revoked in 2026. A token copied out of a cache could stay usable just as long, well after the cache itself is gone.

Keeping Credentials Out of the GitHub Actions Cache

The very best protection is to stop any credentials from getting cached in the first place. Only relevant folders should be cached, the ones that hold dependencies and build outputs that take time and effort to restore without caching. Complete home directories and workspaces should never be cached, because they’re more likely to hold secrets.

Good housekeeping habits like logging out and clearing credentials before caching anything can help prevent caching secrets. OpenID Connect (OIDC) provides temporary cloud credentials, instead of long-lasting access keys that can be exploited by pull requests.

At the same time, limit possible exposure for secrets that are already in caches. Set external contributors to require manual approval for workflows, to reduce the risk of malicious pull requests. By default, GitHub only requires this approval for first-time contributors, so it reduces the risk without removing it. Make sure to regularly review caches for secrets that might have been exposed and replace those credentials before deleting the unsafe cache.

Treat Every Cached Path as Shared

The cache is shared more widely than the secrets are. A workflow that can’t see a single secret can still restore whatever main has cached, so the safe working assumption is that every cached path is readable by anyone who can open a pull request. Decide what goes into the cache on that basis, and keep credentials out of it.

item.title: 29 Fake Bank Sites Caught Using the Same Contact Details to Steal Logins
item.description:
A bank doesn’t necessarily need a real branch, banking licence, or even a genuine business to look convincing online anymore. A phishing campaign Netskope Threat Labs discovered reveals that cybercriminals can create fictional but genuine-looking banks, with account-opening pages, customer support details, and online banking portals, using just a ready-made PHP script.

Researchers report that around 29 fake-bank domains appeared over seven weeks- starting in late September 2026- using names like Sunray Trust, Quartz Bank, Western Future Bank and Apex Trust Financial Bank. item.title: F5 Patches Two NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities, One Dating Back to (2015)
item.description:
F5 has released security updates for two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, the open-source web server owned and maintained by F5, powering more than 225 million websites.

These vulnerabilities can allow attackers to execute code on affected servers without authentication, exposing websites, APIs and the applications running behind them. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 with a CVSS score of 9.2.

What’s interesting is that they were independently investigated and reported to F5 by five research teams, including Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7 and Xint. Per their findings, both flaws are in NGINX’s HTTP/2 implementation and not in the websites or applications using the software.

Wiz’s research, shared with Hackread.com, provides a detailed overview of the security impact of the issue. Wiz researchers used the AI-powered Wiz Atlas platform to identify the flaws and Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate their findings.

They successfully carried out remote code execution (RCE) on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. This included a server delivering ordinary static files without a backend application or third-party modules. Both vulnerabilities, however, require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected server.

The NGINX disclosures come just a day after the discovery of Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)- a critical OpenJDK vulnerability reported by Calif that can also lead to unauthenticated remote code execution.


The Vulnerabilities


CVE-2026-123007 is an integer underflow in HTTP/2 flow-control accounting. It affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5, released in 2015. Incorrect handling of unused data allowances can eventually cause an out-of-bounds memory operation.

The other flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting versions 1.19.7 to 1.31.8. It can occur during reverse-proxy processing when NGINX runs low on available connection slots.


NGINX is a recurring target


This isn’t the first time NGINX has faced attacks involving AI-assisted vulnerability research. In May, Hackread.com reported attacks exploiting NGINX Rift (CVE-2026-42945). That flaw was different, though, because it required a specific, non-default rewrite configuration and mainly exposed servers to denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, whereas RCE was possible only when ASLR was disabled or bypassed.

The latest vulnerabilities are far riskier because they let unauthenticated attackers execute code on affected servers. A successful attack can give them control over systems handling traffic for multiple websites and applications and this would put customer data and services at risk.

Patches and Updates


In its November 18 security update, F5 addressed ten NGINX vulnerabilities, including additional flaws affecting HTTP/3, the DNS resolver and mail proxy modules, and issues that could cause DoS or other security problems. The fixes address both critical HTTP/2 flaws.

Administrators should update NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 (stable) or 1.31.9 (mainline). NGINX Plus users should install the applicable fixed version: 37.0.7.1, 37.0.8.1, 37.2.0.1, or 37.3.0.1.

Those unable to upgrade immediately should temporarily disable HTTP/2 using http2 off in affected server blocks.
For defenders, the key takeaway is that finding vulnerabilities is only half the job; now, they also need to identify affected systems and get the fixes installed before attackers can exploit them.
